blocks.x: I'll make a note on here that we're interviewing Mr. Eddie Dawson at his home at 325 North Robertson and the date is June. No, not North Robertson, North Johnson. Johnson, I'll finally get it. North Johnson, yeah. I got the number wrong last night.
325 North.

325 North Johnson and this is Bill Russell and Ralph Collins is here and the date is June the 28th, 1961. Well, I think I would have, Dick Allen just stopped by and I said what can we ask Mr. Dawson? He said ask about the time that the King Oliver used to drop the brick or something.

What was that for? That was for the, to give you a notice to stop playing, you know. When you, the boys when they knock off, they keep on playing over, you know, couple of strings, couple of bars over the beat, over the knockoff and well, he just got a big brick and when he got ready to knock off he throw the brick down on the music stand and see I guess you'll hear that. He really did that, huh? Yeah, he did that. I don't think he was kissing. No, no, he did that, yeah.
Why didn't the boys want to stop?

Well, they'd forget, you know, that he'd knock off, you know, they had a way of knocking off with the leader, knock off with his foot when he getting ready to stop. But when he'd knock off they'd be feeling so good, you know, that they couldn't stop, you know, they wouldn't hear him when he knocked off, you see. And then he'd have to first stand to get a brick then to make a noise so he'd knock off.
Did he keep it on his chair or something?

He had to right alongside him, yeah, by his chair. Yeah, yeah, throw it down. Where were y'all playing at? Oh, we was playing, let's see, we was playing Uptown, I forget the name of that hall now. It's, uh, I can't think of the name of that hall, it's Uptown somewhere. Uh, uh, that's, that's what I should have found out the name. It's been so long, you know.
Where was that located?
Here's Jackson or Rappen, Boston? Uh, it was up on, uh, on, uh, let's see, between, on, on, Rome between 6 and 7.
I don't know, I think.
Somewhere up that way. Somewhere up that way. Up around that way, yeah.
There used to be the Providence Hall up in there. Yeah. Of course the Longshoremen, that's on the Jacksonville.
Let's see, wait now.
6 and 7, you mean 6 and 7 hundred block?
Yeah, uh, between 6th Street. Oh, I see, yeah. That's far up, yeah. Oh, I see, yeah. It was, yeah.

Oh, how do I think of it? Uh, there's a hall of Richard M. Jones, they used to call him Miney Jones, the piano player. Uh, oh yeah, yeah. He told me once that, uh, Bolden and some of the old time bands played at a place called Tintight Hall. Did you ever hear of that? Tintight.
Tintop. Tintop. That was on, uh.
Tintop? I thought he said Tintight. Tintop. Tintop. Tintroof.
Tintop.
Maybe he did say Tintop. Tintop.
Tintop, yeah.
Tintop, yeah.
Tintop, yeah. Where was that?
That was on Pedida. Pedida between, uh, between, uh, Franklin and Liberty Franklin. Tintop. Tintop. On the left hand side. Small hall, eh? Still in? Oh, no, that thing is gone. Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah. It wouldn't have been Kenny's Hall, the one they called Quenky Butt Hall.
Kenny?
There's a church later. Would you read that?
That was, uh, Kenny's Hall. That was, that was on Pedida Street, too. Yeah, that was on the floor then. Yeah. Yeah.
Tintop. Did it have a Tintop?

No, well, it had a, yes, it had a tin roof, you know, on top, and, uh, when it rained, you could hear the noise, you know, they called it the Tintop. Ha, ha, ha. It, uh, Kenny's Hall, and, uh, they called it the Funky Butt, you know?
How did it get that name ready, do you know?
Just made it up amongst them people out in front of town, you know. Uh-huh.
Oh, uh, this other Tintop Hall, is that near where the Zulu's Club was, remember?
Yes, right in that same... The Ruchach's Saloon was in the corner. Right, the Ruchach's on the corner, right in the middle of the block, that's where it was at, yeah.
That's where it was at, yeah. On the same side of the street?
Yeah, that's right.
Yeah, I never saw that. I saw the Zulu's Club and a few other buildings.
Well, the Zulu's Club was right on that...
Yeah, I remember that. Uh-huh. I have a picture of that.
Yeah.
Uh, you say it was just a small hall, Eddie?
Yes, it wasn't such a large place.
Was it one of those halls where the band goes up on the balcony, or did it have a little bandstand?
No, it had a bandstand. Uh-huh. It didn't have no balcony, no...
Like the Artesian Hall?
Yeah, yeah.
Small hall, eh? But it wasn't up in there, up in the...
It wasn't behind the stairs, up on the balcony, wasn't up there?

No, no. Oh, that was the Pelican, like, was on Rampard and Gravia. That was, that had a stairs that go up. Balcony in front. Yeah. That's where we, uh, me and Kid Rene was playing it. We played there. I played there with Rene at the Pelican. On Rampard between, uh, Neb Gravia. Yes, I know by Neb Gravia. Well, we had, well, Beansy was running that place. But they had a front porch down on the gallery, you see? And we used to go out and play a couple of numbers out on that front gallery before we'd go in and play, you know, the dance style, the dance style. The avatar.
Yeah. Well, I was gonna ask again, that Oliver band with Joe Oliver, who else was in that? Can you remember, who else played with him in those days when you were working with him?
Well, he had, uh, he had Chris Minor playing the drum. Chris Minor was on the drum. And he had, uh, George Foster, Pop Foster on the bass. And I played guitar.
You were playing guitar.
Yeah, I played violin with him, you know. I didn't stay with him long. And, uh, he had Willie Foster playing violin. That's George Foster's brother.
We got him up in Baton Rouge, remember Ralph?

Yeah. And, uh, Eddie Atkins was playing trombone. Oh, yeah. Eddie Atkins. And, uh, let's see, Joe, Joe was on the trumpet. And, uh, let's see, Ed. Uh, clarinet, let's see who. He had a clarinet, uh, C. Now he had, uh, Willie, Willie Caput, uh, Chris Minor, and Pop Foster. And he had a clarinet, I think. Uh, uh, I don't know if he was just for his name now. Uh, Lorenzo Teale. and he had a clarinet Lorenzo Teal Lorenzo Teal
Did they have any name for the band? Is it Joe's band? Magnolia band
Magnolia, the Magnolia band
That was Lorenzo Teal, Jr. Yeah Yeah, yeah

Now he leaves, after he left there he joined with Louis Armstrong and went away and they had a band together they went up the line up to Chicago they had a band together Joe Oliver and Louis Armstrong double up together Well the only one man he'd taken with him that was Pop Foster Yeah The bass player Yeah, when he left They changed, they had all Louis had all different men when they went up there they went together
Yeah That was about the time of the First World War
Yeah, well that was at that was at Liberty in Ivoryville at Hunts and Nagels Dancehall
Oh, I've heard of that bar
That's where we was playing at that was somewhere around about 1915 I think it is 1912
When you were playing with the
That was 1912, yeah That was about the time it was That was Hunts and Nagels
How's that name spelled? I never get to see it
I spelled it N-E-A-G-E-L Nagle Hunts H-U-N-T-Z Nagle Yeah You see there was two partners One was named Hunts and one was named Nagle
Well I thought it was one big name
No, two names There was two Hunts One fella named Hunts and the other fella named Nagle There was two
Oh, Hunts and Nagle
Yeah, Hunts and Nagle Hunts and Nagle
Yeah, I never do that That was one name
Hunts and Nagle Hunts and Nagle That was I thought it was one name That was one word
Funny how we got the wrong idea Yeah You know it and somebody writes it up in the book Yeah, yeah That's why we want to talk to you fellas and remember everything
Yeah, yeah, that's right Try to get it straight Uh huh

That's good Last time we were talking with you I think I asked you this question But I'd like to ask you again Uh I wonder if you can remember The names of those old bands that were going About the same time that Buddy Bowling had a band Can you remember the names of those bands in those days?

Well, they had the blaze away band The blaze away they had Let me see Well, Eureka The blaze away And The Let's see The The Olympia The Olympia The blaze away The The Tuxedo Eureka I mean they had the They had uh Let me see now
Are these the brass bands you're talking about?

Oh, well, no Well, they was They was string bands String bands Yeah Of course they had They had a couple of them With the names of brass bands too Uh huh But they was They had the They had regular dance bands called You know Eureka band And you know Yeah
Who was in that blaze away band?
Blaze away? That was a Creole band from downtown Amongst all Creole fellas, you know They didn't have no more than about four or five pieces in it
Do you remember him the leader or anybody who played in it?
I don't know I don't know who they are now, you know But I remember that name They did have a band by that name
So you were very young then, I guess When you started to play then?
I never played with none of them
I never remember that before you Yeah And you remember how they sounded? Was it much different?
It was a regular Dixieland band like we played Yeah About the same style
Was there any difference between the downtown and the uptown bands or styles? No it wasn't

No it wasn't They all played They practically played all that Dixieland stuff, you know Yeah Jazz music, you know Yeah Like Buddy and all and Joe Oliver and all of them They all played that jazz music, Dixieland stuff, see
Somebody told me one time they played more blues uptown than they did down Only one band
Only one band Only one that used to play the most that played the blues was Chris Kelly Chris Kelly
Chris Kelly

Chris Kelly band was about the only band that used to play the blues All of them Practically everything he played sounded like the blues Yeah But he could blow, he could blow Yeah He could play it People was crazy about his band
Yeah Well he'd come along a little later, wouldn't he?

Well, no he was active in that time when Around the time that I'm telling you about now When Billy Phillips and all them places was running, you know Yeah The Hunts and Nagel When they was running, he was operating that was around 1912 He was playing then he had a good band Cause I played with his band I played tenor banjo with him for a good while Oh yeah Chris Kelly had He had all that work over the river He was playing over the river And of course, played white and colored dancers too But the majority of his work was for colors And all this advertising and techniques and all the things He got most all that there He just kept, he had practically he had a dance for every night in the week Just like René
Yeah, on Static

He had a band just like René had But I believe René had the best band You know, he had a better band He was more of a blue player, you see Just like I said, he played blues But René had played classical and blues too, you see So Yeah, he had the He was playing about that time
Can you tell us any more about the About the time when the district was running About that time you were talking about Do you remember the different bands that were playing in the district?
Well around about 1904 They had O'Neal Lavish there He had a five piece band He was playing at Few Clothes Right on Franklin Near Iberville
Is that the place that they crossed from the 25? Right across from the 25
They had a fella, a big fella called Few Clothes It was a dance hall
Yeah, I know F.S. He played there

Yeah, yeah, I know Neal Lavish there He played, you know, he was a violin player Oh, he violin That was his band Yeah, it was his band And that fella Few Clothes had his dance hall there And then the next block from there Was Harry Park and Charlie Park Called 101 Ranch And that's where I played there
That must have been around 1907. Harry Parker's dance hall, that's a... Was that the 101 Ranch? 101 Ranch, me and Manetta. Mani Manetta.
He played there with you?

Yeah, that was my job. I had Mani Manetta. Who else did you? I had the old man, Umprey. Willie Umprey, the clarinet player, yeah. And I had a Mani Manetta on the piano, and I was playing guitar. That time I was playing guitar. And John Vino on the drum. And... Let's see, we only had five pieces. See, I count five. Mani Manetta, Willie Umprey, John Vino, myself, and the piano.
Did you have a carnet in those days?
No, we didn't have...we didn't have...we didn't have a carnet then.
Didn't use carnet in the district?

No, no, no, no, not around that time. I was the one that...I was the first one that started to bring in the carnet in there. Freddie Kep would come through there with his carnet one night. And Mr. Harry Parker was standing in the door, and Freddie had played a job. It was kind of late. Almost time for us to knock off. And Freddie came in with his trumpet and laid it down, you know. And so Harry Parker would come and ask me what instrument that was. And I told him to do the carnet. They said, well, tell him to go ahead and tune up and play a piece with you. So I told him, I said, well, you know, they don't allow you to blow that instrument around, you know, now around here. He said, oh, he said, tell him to go ahead and...so I asked Fred, I said, you want to play a couple of numbers from the boss wants you to play? He said, well, if he takes care of me, I don't mind. And the police was standing in the door, well, he'd be there every night. So Harry Parker said, oh, go ahead and play. That's all right. They ain't going to do you nothing. They ain't going to put you in jail. I'll be, hold me responsible. Freddie said, all right, boss. And he took his carnet out and tuned up with us and went to play. And it sounds so good, all the women that was beer hustling down at Hunts and Nagels there, they heard about it and they start to leave and the crowd was leaving. They're coming over to Harry Parker's place. Well, after the packed and jam his place, he asked Fred if he wanted to work every night with us. And he said, yes, if you get a permit. So he said, well, I'll go to the mayor, see the mayor tomorrow and I'll get a permit. And you'll be here tomorrow night at the Dawson's Band. And after that, well, he, the next day, Harry Parker went and got a permit for the trumpet. And he worked there with us then from that on. And that's before Joe Oliver then went to Hunts and Nagels. But the next following week, Hunts and Nagels then got Joe Oliver's whole band over there.
Oh, yeah.
Then after I quit, you see, over there went to Joe Oliver. That's all.
Did you have a violin in your band that everyone wanted to?
Um, yeah, we did. That's right. We had, we had Jimmy Palau. Oh, yeah. Jimmy Palau played Bobby. I believe he's dead.
Yeah, I never really get the door ever hearing.
Too bad. You were speaking about this O'Neal Lavasheaux, is that his name? Lavasheaux, yeah. Lavasheaux. Yeah, O'Neal Lavasheaux. Can you remember, how many was in his, it was a string band, though?
Yeah, he's a regular dance band, you know. Is it a fire piece, do you think? Fire piece, yeah. Violin, uh, violin, guitar, bass, and, no, didn't have no bass. They had drum and piano.
Oh, they had a drum?
Yeah, drum and piano.
Oh. You don't know any of the men that were playing, besides the...

Well, I'll tell you, he never had no standard men, you know. He just, uh, sometime, you know, he'd change in different men, you know, half of the time. Uh-oh. Because, uh, at that time, there was so much work going on, you had a hard time keeping a man on one job, you know. Saying, like, this week he'd have a man, and next week he'd have a different man all the time. That's the way he was, you see. Couldn't keep a man on, cause the job wasn't that big, you know. And the tips wasn't that good there, you see. And the fellas, musicians, was jumping from band to band. Anytime they'd get a good opening where they had more money to be made, that was jumping. That's the way it was going. They were running from one... Couldn't keep a good man in one spot. Well, he'd had his place over there, the tips wasn't so much at few close places, you see. And, uh, dead bull, they ain't work, make a night or two nights, and after that, then... Gone, you know, you'd have to get another man, you see.
Did, uh, was it a regular thing to have drums in the band?

Oh, practically most all the bands had drums. Oh, they did have drums? Yeah, that was the main instrument, a drum. Piano and drum, they always had that. Oh, did they? Yeah, they never did, they'd be without that drum. Oh. Out of all the time when they didn't have no blowing instruments, they used to have to have that drum, see.
What did they have, like a snare drum or... Regular, regular... Snare and bass?

Bass and snare drum, yeah, trap drum and bass drum, too, you see, yeah. And, uh, so from that on, after that, why, they, uh, the district, then they started to have all that blowing instruments, you see. And, uh, there was so much knowledge. You take Harry Parker, Harry Parker 101 Ranch, and, uh, uh, Hunts and Nagels, them was large places. Large dance halls. They had, they had women with, uh, what was employed there, just to sell a beer, you know. Big quarts of beer, and them, them chummies off the ships used to come through there, you know. Them Norwegian ships would come in port, and them fellas would come in, and, uh, that's the first place they'd go. One of them dance halls, and get in there and spend them on a drink and have a good time. They had a lot, a lot of time, we used to have our collection, Kitty Box, they called it. And, uh, we'd find ten dollar gold pieces in there instead of thinking. They was copper cents. These fellas would just go in their pocket and have all that change, you know. Gold money in it. And when we'd go to, and Maggie Mineta would tell you, when we'd go to whack up in the morning, we'd have ten dollar gold pieces in there. What they'd take for, for, uh, copper cents, you see.
Why do they call them chummies? Those are the sailors?

Yeah, sailors off the ships. Them time the ships would point into this port, you know, from the foreign ships, you know, coming in. Them Norwegian ships most so, they'd come in loaded down, you know. And the time they'd get in this, they'd pay off when they hit sea, you see. And them guys would be out of the sea, maybe, for three or four months like that, before they'd hear the port, you see. When they'd get here, they'd have plenty of money.
Oh.
And they'd say, it was a good time then. Yeah.
Yeah, it must have been a good time. Uh, that Blaze Away band, you say, was a downtown band?

Downtown, I'll tell you now, I'll tell you who can probably give you a little more idea about that band, more better than me, cause he'd come down the Creole part of the town. That's, uh, uh, what you call, uh, Harold. Harold Dejon.
Harold Dejon. We see him quite often, yeah.
Now, Harold Dejon tell you about that Blaze Away band down there. I know they had a Blaze Away, but, uh, I just, uh...
Were you from, uh, more from the Uptown, uh, section?
Yeah, I was most from Uptown, see. There I come up, I come up in that, in the Third Ward, see. I just moved down in this Fort Ward since, uh, 31.
You were up there most of the time?
Most of the time I was up, Uptown, up there in the Third Ward.
Okay, the Third Ward was all around Perdido Street up there.
Yeah, around Perdido Street, that.
Well, you'd remember, uh, did you remember bands like the Galloway band?
Galloway, yes. I even played a couple jobs with them, with Galloway. I played guitar with Galloway. He was the one-legged bass player.
Oh, bass player.

Yeah, he was the bass player. He had one leg walk with one crutch. Oh. Wasn't that Charlie Galloway, was it? Uh, yeah, I believe it was Charlie Galloway. I think that was his first name, Charlie Galloway.
I heard somebody call him Happy Galloway.

Oh, he had, uh, well, that was, uh, that was the name of the band, Happy Galloway's band. Oh, I see. Because, see, it was his band. It went by his name. He had a barber shop on here on, on Baltimore between Pardis and Lafayette. He had a barber shop.
Yeah.
And that was his band.
Can you remember who was band?
Uh, he had, well, he had, um, he had, well, he first, when Kid Punch first came here from the country, the trumpet player, he had Kid Punch with him.
I didn't know that we see Punch all the time.
I don't remember that. Yeah, ask him. Just ask him about Galloway. Yeah, we'll ask him. Uh-huh. And, uh, he had, he had a pretty good band. He had Frankie Doosen on trombone.
Yeah.
Yeah. And, uh, Joe Welch on the violin.
Joe Welch.

Joe Welch, he was a good drummer, but he played violin too, see. Oh, I see. Yeah. In that time, Galloway was getting plenty of work too, you know. Uh-huh. But, a whole lot of country work out of, up, all up the Southern Pacific, TP, all up there. Oh, yeah. A lot of country jobs, just people used to, you know, hire bands that go up in the country there. Yeah. And that kept him busy all the time. Always going in the country, see, band. But he kept busy, though.
Another, another name, uh, Olivia. Yeah.
It was Adam Olivier, from uptown. Olivia. Up on Chappapulis. I know Buck Johnson used to talk about him. Olivier. I think he played violin, the, uh, leader. He was a barber too. I can't.
Maybe too many. Olivia. But they had Tony Jackson played piano with him.

For a while, when he was a kid. And Buck started out with him. Up near, uh, near Amelia in the Chappapulis. I think they had a barber shop. Uh, do you remember the Peyton band? Peyton. I forget his first name. I think he was an accordion player.

Oh, yeah, Peyton. He had a, flute in, a chord in. He used to play, uh, well he didn't have no band. He just had, he used to use that flute, that chord in and the guitar, you know, complimenting. Not a big band, huh? No, he didn't have no big band. Just, just them two pieces. Never used no drum or nothing. Just that chord. Yeah. Lee Peyton. Lee Peyton. Lee Peyton, yeah. He played the chord in. Flutina called it a great, you know, one of those big chordings, you know. Oh, yeah. And he used to play up here, when they had the, call it the Bucket of Blood up there around, you know where 25's used to kick at the ham up there. Oh, yeah, 25?
Yeah. That was the big name for it? Bucket of Blood.
Yeah. Yeah.
The 25's is called Bucket of Blood. Yeah, that's right.
They used to call it the Bucket of Blood. Long time. That was before that, before they got 25, before they call it 25.
I thought maybe there's another place like up on Poirier Street or up in the battlefield or someplace up there.
No, no. That was the big 25? Yeah, yeah, around there. I don't believe that. They used to have time.
What, what was that ham kick? What was the idea of that?
Oh, they're just women just kick their legs up and they call it kicking the ham, you know. Oh, yeah. And they get feeling good, you know. Yeah. Yeah.
They really had a ham up there, did they?
Um, I don't, yes they did. I think they did have a ham hanging up on the string up in there. Yeah. Yeah, I'll tell you them, for a long time. So.
I was going to ask some more about your instrument that you started on. What did you start on? Guitar?
Guitar. Guitar. Yeah. I started on the guitar and after I put the guitar down I picked up tenor banjo.
About how old were you when you started on the guitar?
I was about 30, about 30, 33 something. You didn't start when you were a boy then?
No, no, no.
I had a good age when I, and I played the banjo then after the banjo then I'd take no bass violin.
When did you take up the bass do you remember about, was it time of the war or?

Around just about, just about the time of the war. Around 1917, yeah, around, no, around 1912. Before the war. Yeah, before the war I'd take no bass. And from then on I'd play bass, right on. Now and then I'd play, you know, if I catch a job you see, I'd play banjo in between you see, because I never did play study with, you know I'd play study with a band one time and then another fella hired me you know like that. My band wouldn't have enough work all the time to keep me busy. Somebody always wanted a hymn in a different band you see. Well I just kept on playing for the fella who wanted a hymn on the tenor banjo. I had my instrument right there, I'd just pick it up and go and play the job with it you see. But I practically just got so I just put it down all together you see. And sold it, I sold it to Achey. You know a little Achey? Sure. He's the one bought my tenor banjo for me.

I had a good one too. I let him have it. I got tired of being bothered with it, you know. And practically most when I was using it, they would always come from me for congo day to play on them trucks, you know. And I got tired of going on them jobs on it. The weather got so bad and I'd be sitting up on them trucks playing that banjo, I just got tired of doing that and I just put it down. I said I'll get rid of the banjo when the fellas want to hire me. They couldn't get me.
The bass is hard to carry around though too. It has disadvantages too.

Yeah, well, they wasn't using too much bass for the congo parade. Yeah, that's right. Most of the use, you know, plenty, they'd like, the instrumentation they were practically using would be drum, tenor, banjo, cornet, trombone, something like that, clarinet. And they'd be satisfied. Five, four, five pieces like that, they'd be satisfied, you see. The bass was so awkward to be carrying on them trucks. You had to get them trucks high, you got to be carrying it up and down on them trucks. So, it was too inconvenient. Then the weather got, come as it's getting bad and getting so cold and you'd have to be clocking up with coats and things on. You couldn't be too stuffed up to be playing in. Half of the time, you'd have to stand up to play the bass, you see. Sure. And them trucks, they want you to be playing while the trucks is going, you see. Long time ago, they wouldn't, they didn't want that. They'd let you wait until they make a stop.
Did you do much picking in the old days, Eddie?

Yeah, practically, I started off with a bow. You know what I mean? The bass? Yeah. I started off with a bow, too. But, I did more picking after, you know. I started right down. I believe I'm the first one that started that four-four rhythm. I had a way used to pick with one finger, you see. Yeah. That four-four rhythm and that's where it popped for. George Foster, he caught it for me and from that on, all the rest of them started it. Oh, what was it before, Eddie? There you go.
Okay, it's going again. You were talking about the bass and picking.
Yeah, all of the bands practically used to use bows, bass-filing bows. They used to play with more bass with their bows than picking, you see.
Well, when they played with that bow, what would they be playing? They wouldn't be playing four-four?
Yeah, they'd play dance, regular dance. It's like they're playing now with the coaster. They're just using the bow instead of thumping it with their fingers, you see.
But it was still the same...
Yeah, same time, yes. The same time.
Well, what does the picking do? It makes it more...

It makes it, I don't know, more jazz, you know. Yeah, most staccato. Yeah, like that. Better than the bow, you see. Now, they still use bows on these big bands now. They have to... Some of these numbers, they got to use the bow on them, you know. Because the sentimental pieces, you know, it requires the bow. Yeah. And the baseball players now with all these big bands, it's playing that kind of type of music now. They use the bow and then put it down, take them, turn it around on their finger then, when they get to a part where they have to pick, you know.
Did you say, you say, sentimental tunes, like waltzes and things like that?

Well, they have some waltzes, they have to... it goes better with the vocals, better with them waltzes too, you see. But it's something like... the songs like you're singing, you see, like vocal songs, like those fellas women singing or like that, you know.
They're something like Stardust.

Yes, it requires... it sounds better with a bow, you know, than picking with your fingers. Because it's a slow... it's a different type of time. Different time that you've got to give. You can't use that four-four rhythm with that, you see. You got... you got different time that comes in and calls for that vocal stuff, you see.
Well, I was gonna ask some more about your teachers. If you're on your guitar, have you started that? Did you have a teacher or take lessons?
No, I just took it up myself. Never had no teacher at all. I just took it up myself.
Did you get a book or anything to help or just...

segments.title: Opening: recording at Dawson's home, June 28, 1961
segments.summary: Russell notes the address and date; Ralph Collins is present, and a visitor suggested asking about King Oliver and the brick.

segments.title: King Oliver dropping a brick to signal the band to stop
segments.summary: Dawson explains Oliver threw a brick on the music stand to cut off players who ran past the knock-off; the hall was uptown, name forgotten.

segments.title: Pinning down the uptown hall's location
segments.summary: Russell and Dawson try to place the hall on Rome Street between 6th and 7th.

segments.title: Tin Top Hall, Kenny's Hall (Funky Butt) and Perdido Street halls
segments.summary: Dawson identifies Tin Top as a small hall on Perdido with a tin roof, nearby Kenny's Hall called the Funky Butt, and the Zulu Club.

segments.title: Hall layouts and playing at the Pelican with Kid Rene
segments.summary: Bandstand versus balcony halls; Dawson and Kid Rene played the Pelican, starting on the front gallery.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: Personnel of Joe Oliver's Magnolia band
segments.summary: Dawson names Chris Minor, Pop Foster, Willie Foster, Eddie Atkins, Oliver and a clarinetist (Lorenzo Tio) in the Magnolia band; he played briefly.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: Oliver leaving for Chicago; Hunts and Nagle dance hall
segments.summary: Oliver went north with Armstrong taking Pop Foster; Dawson recalls Hunts and Nagle's hall around 1912 and corrects the spelling of the two partners' names.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: Names of early bands and downtown versus uptown style
segments.summary: Dawson recalls Blaze Away, Eureka, Olympia and Tuxedo; the Blaze Away was a small Creole band and all played similar Dixieland.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: Chris Kelly's blues band and Kid Rene
segments.summary: Chris Kelly was the one blues band; Dawson played tenor banjo with him around 1912; Rene had the best band.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: 101 Ranch and bringing Freddie Keppard's cornet into the district
segments.summary: Dawson recalls O'Neal Lavasheaux's band, then his own five-piece band at Harry Parker's 101 Ranch and how Keppard got a permit to play cornet.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: Lavasheaux's string band and unsteady personnel
segments.summary: The violinist's band had no standard men; musicians jumped bands for better tips.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: Drums, big dance halls and sailors' tips
segments.summary: Drums were standard; Hunts and Nagle and the 101 Ranch drew Norwegian sailors whose tips included gold pieces.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: Blaze Away band, Harold Dejan and living uptown
segments.summary: Dawson refers Collins to Harold Dejan for the downtown Creole band, and says he grew up in the Third Ward around Perdido.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: Happy Galloway's band and country work
segments.summary: Dawson played guitar with Galloway, a one-legged bass player and barber, whose band included Kid Punch, Frankie Dusen and Joe Welch.

segments.chapter: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
segments.title: Olivier, Lee Peyton and the Bucket of Blood
segments.summary: Quick notes on Olivier's band, Lee Peyton's flutina and guitar duo, and the Bucket of Blood and kicking the ham.

segments.title: Guitar, tenor banjo and bass; leaving banjo for parade trucks
segments.summary: Dawson began guitar around age 30, then banjo and bass, and gave up banjo after rides on parade trucks.

segments.title: Bowing versus picking the bass
segments.summary: Dawson claims to have started the four-four picked rhythm; bows suit waltzes and vocal numbers.

segments.title: Learning music: method books, a white teacher and Hippolyte Charles's band
segments.summary: Self-taught, with method books and chord charts from a bass teacher; he learned to read from Joe Welsh and Louis Cantrell in Hippolyte Charles's band.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles and the country clubs
segments.title: Hippolyte Charles's band at the country club
segments.summary: Personnel, the country-club and Lions Club contracts, Charles's heart trouble, Charlie Love replacing him, and tea dances at union pay.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson as a substitute trumpeter
segments.summary: Dawson says Bunk sat in for others and never led his own band.

segments.title: Edward Clem's country band and replacing Bob Lyons
segments.summary: Dawson joined Clem's Pelican band on bass, took Bob Lyons's place, travelled the railroad, and describes Clem and Joe Alva as readers.

segments.title: Clem's background; John Pendleton and Joe Oliver's limits
segments.summary: Clem's name and origins; Oliver recommended trombonist John Pendleton for a St. Charles dance job.

segments.title: Wooden Joe and the small spot on Claiborne and Tulane
segments.summary: Dawson played tenor banjo in a little band with Wooden Joe, Manuel Gabriel and Sammy Penn.

segments.title: Trumpeter Ned and small uptown bands
segments.summary: Dawson cannot place Ned and mentions small bands around the Garden District.

segments.title: String bands versus orchestras
segments.summary: Bands under six or seven pieces were string bands, playing ragtime in a hillbilly manner.

segments.title: Willie Edwards and Kid Punch
segments.summary: Dawson never worked with Edwards and says Punch came from Raceland.

segments.title: Freddie Keppard on violin and picnics with Manuel Perez
segments.summary: Keppard started on violin and took up a horn at picnics; Sidney Bechet's trouble with a train and wine is told.

segments.title: Playing in the houses with guitar and mandolin
segments.summary: Dawson says houses mostly hired pianos; he sometimes went round with a rich young man's band; Frank Landry and others played there.

segments.title: Early district pianists
segments.summary: Dawson names Alfred Wilson, Tony Jackson and Robert Caldwell, none of whom he worked with.

segments.chapter: Rene, Whitney Bank and early life
segments.title: Whitney Bank job and where Dawson was born
segments.summary: Dawson worked 41 years at Whitney Bank from 1917 and was born on Mandeville Street; Russell asks about Papa Laine.

segments.chapter: Rene, Whitney Bank and early life
segments.title: Kid Rene's pupils and bass-playing with Rene
segments.summary: Sharkey learned from Rene; Dawson played bass with Rene, with breakups, and hears of Simon Marrero and bazooka bands.

segments.chapter: Rene, Whitney Bank and early life
segments.title: Serenading string bands and Galloway's repertoire
segments.summary: Boys' string bands serenaded at night; Galloway played ragtime and waltzes.

segments.title: First blues, Buddy Bolden and Walter Preston
segments.summary: Dawson recalls Bolden's blues band at Cole's lawn, singer Rabbit Brown and Walter Preston, who was drafted at about fifty.

segments.title: Best guitar players and the mandolin contest
segments.summary: Philip Nickerson and Frank Landry were top guitarists; Dawson won a mandolin contest in the French Quarter.

segments.title: George Jones's band, the Johnson-Jeffries fight night and collections
segments.summary: Dawson played for George Jones, who kept the collection; they played on the night of the Johnson fight.

segments.title: Trip to Indianapolis with George Jones for the Shriners
segments.summary: The band played the Claypool Hotel for several nights; Dawson declined an offer to stay, staying near home.

segments.title: Playing bass drum in parades; brass bands and funerals
segments.summary: Dawson played bass drum with Edward Clem in Plaquemine; he preferred string and dance music and funerals lacked bands then.

segments.chapter: Hippolyte Charles and the country clubs
segments.title: Hippolyte Charles again: country club band and pay
segments.summary: Charles was a first-class trumpeter; Dawson repeats the country-club band lineup and two-dollar-an-hour pay.

segments.chapter: Uptown versus downtown styles and Tom Anderson's
segments.title: Ragtime versus Dixieland, uptown versus downtown, and the blues
segments.summary: Downtown bands read music and played waltzes and quadrilles; uptown played blues by ear.

segments.title: Rene's booking book and ending
segments.summary: Rene's wife kept bookings; Russell announces a couple of minutes left and asks about Tom Anderson's.

segments.title: Tom Anderson's place and tips from Norwegian sailors; goodbye
segments.summary: Dawson describes the Basin and Iberville place, bandmates Tom Brown and Sam Moran, tips and gold pieces from sailors; the interview closes.
